This article addresses patients’ perspectives on home-based rehabilitation exercises following total hip arthroplasty (THA). The topic is investigated through a qualitative method using semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using thematic analysis. The study found the theme: 'wishing to return to the well-known everyday life', and the subtheme 'general physical activity versus rehabilitation exercise'. The topic of the paper is interesting and overall the paper is well-written; however, there are a number of issues throughout the paper.

We confirm that we have read this submission and believe that we have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

The paper tackles an interesting problem. However, the novelty is limited: the proposed method is a straightforward combination of two existing techniques. The writing is also difficult to follow in Sections 3-4, with undefined notation. On the positive side, the experimental evaluation is thorough, covering five datasets with proper ablations.

This is a well written review of the role of antihypertensive medication in patients with COVID-19. There have however been several prior papers pointing out the role of hypertension in COVID-19 and the relative risk of various antihypertensive medications. It would therefore be important to point out what new information this paper provides.

It might also be of value to discuss the role of obesity, since obesity is a risk factor for COVID-19 and often co-exists with hypertension.

In regards to the the effect of the individual classes of antihypertensive medications in patients with COVID-19, it should be emphasized that the number of patients is rather small and that therefore no definitive conclusions can be drawn. It might be of interest to present statistical power calculations for the sample size that would be needed to reach a significant conclusion in regard to the risk of the individual agents in patients with COVID-19.

Without further explanation of what is new in this paper to justify publication, I do not believe it has sufficient priority for indexing.

In this article, the authors present an open-source platform called Sherlock, which can be very useful for computational biologists working with a lot of different datasets within one or several projects. The platform is designed to make use of well-known resources and concepts such as Docker, and PrestoDB. Sherlock is easily extendable and can be used both on a local computer or in connection with a cloud storage solution. Once Sherlock is properly set up and the needed data sets imported and formatted, the data can be integrated and analyzed using SQL queries as shown in the three simple use cases.

Sherlock can become a great addition to the suite of tools used by computational biologists, especially when it comes to bigger projects involving a lot of public datasets as well as own data generated by collaborators. The article is nicely written and gives a good overview of the Sherlock platform as well as possible use cases. However, it can be further improved in three main aspects as detailed below: making clear who is the target audience, improving the documentation about setting up Sherlock, and improving the flow of the Implementation and Operation section.

Both the title and abstract mention that Sherlock is designed for biologists and only on page 6, the text mentions computational biologists specifically. However, both from the description of the setup and the specific use cases, it seems to me that the actual target audience should be clearly stated as “computational biologists”. It is worth considering changing the “for biology” part in the title since it is not very clear or specific as it is now.

One major concern is that neither the manuscript nor the online documentation seem to describe in enough detail how to set up the data needed for the three presented use cases. There is a nice deployment guide and the use case examples seem reasonable, but the step in-between is missing. The use cases assume that the user has an already configured Sherlock system with the necessary files stored, properly formatted and the right tables created, etc. I specifically checked the GitHub documentation, among others the “Loading … data to Sherlock” sections and I don’t think enough detail is given for a user like me to set it up (and I consider myself a computational biologist). I would need to know which raw data files from STRING were retrieved and stored in the raw zone, how were the JSON files generated that need to be copied to the landing zone, etc. I was able to find the scripts, which should help for this step (
                https://github.com/earlham-sherlock/earlham-sherlock.github.io/tree/master/loaders) but they are also not described in enough detail, especially in connection with the use cases. So, what I think is needed is the following: 
                add a short description to each use case in the manuscript about which databases are needed to execute the example queries;
                    on GitHub, add a step-by-step tutorial for how to set up the specific databases/tables needed for the use cases. For use case 1, the tutorial should include information about how and from what data to create the tables “master.mapping”, ”master.tissues”, ”master.string_proteins”, while for use case 2 and 3, the needed tables are “master.bgee_2020_11_16” and “master.omnipath_2020_10_04”.

For example, the end of paragraph one, which describes the scalability of Docker Swarm, also fits well with the last paragraph of the Overview section. This section could also be renamed to “Overview of the Sherlock platform”.

While a substantial literature is provided on the western population’s expectations/habits regarding the effectiveness of brain training (BT), studies exploring beliefs with respect to BT in different cultural backgrounds are scarce. To fill this gap, the study aimed at investigating the attitudes and the habits of Japanese consumers towards brain training (BT) applications and games. After providing an online-based survey, responses of 818 participants without age limits were analyzed. Results suggest positive beliefs about the effectiveness of BTs, regardless of the level of experience with brain training programs. Moreover, beliefs about the effectiveness of BT were weakly correlated with the number of programs used and its duration, while gender difference about their side effect were reported. The most widely used BT was Brain Age: Train your Brain in a Minutes a Day! (52,93%), a program made by Nintendo.

The issue is of interest since previous beliefs surely impact the intention to use apps and programs for cognitive stimulation. However, in my opinion, authors missed the opportunity to explore other factors (see below) that might have a more profound impact on users’ engagement with trainings programs, and unless they are able to derive from collected data a more nuanced view of why people take part in trainings aimed at enhancing their cognitive abilities, I’m afraid that findings are not worth publishing.

Please, find below my detailed comments.

Abstract

Here, no information was provided for the study aim of the study (which should be shortly described). Furthermore, please mention in the methods subsection that participants were recruited without age limits, that the questionnaire was an online survey and for how long it was available on the platform.

Introduction

- Please, explicitly differentiate brain trainings from cognitive trainings as the latter are represented by “a guided practice on a set of standard tasks designed to increase specific cognitive functions” (Bahar-Fuchs, Clare, Woods, 2013) while the former are mostly based on unstructured activities aimed at a general enhancement of cognitive functioning in a nonspecific manner.

- Please, clarify that a potential enhancement of working memory is crucial for individuals with age-related cognitive decline since such ability is the most significant predictor of functional capacity in daily life.

-When referring to the transfer problem for cognitive trainings please, cite crucial evidence (e.g.: Borella E, et al., 2017 [Ref 1]) demonstrating not only a far transfer of gains from working memory to reasoning abilities, but also the role of individual characteristics (see below) in mediating the effect.

- Authors refer to the TAM (Davies et al., 1989) in order to explain the reason why specific variables (particularly beliefs) were collected and analyzed. However, although perceived usefulness (PU) is one of the two determinants accounting for 60-65% of variance in duration, frequency and intensity of using a technology, PU is determined by two other factors: perceived effectiveness and perceived efficiency. Perceived effectiveness is defined as the degree to which consumers believe that using a technology will provide benefits in performing certain activities (
                performance expectancy, unified theory of acceptance and use of technology -UTAUT-, Venkatesh et al., 2012) while perceived efficiency (
                effort expectancy) is the degree of ease associated with consumers’ use of technology. I understand that none of these variables was considered in the present survey (thus limiting the relevance of the findings) but the authors’ assumption of a direct relationship between participants' beliefs about the effectiveness of brain trainings and their intention to use/actual usage of apps/games for BT is not supported by current TA models. Indeed, maybe participants were not using them just because they did not have any performance expectancy (no perceived usefulness in enhancing their cognitive abilities). Apart from commenting on that, I think that authors should stratify their data according to age (as they did for gender). Indeed, individual differences namely age, gender, and experience are theorized to moderate various AUT relationships and in my opinion, that’s the only way to derive some (potentially) interesting findings from the collected data.
